H1.text: Ten kilograms of rice, plus ten kilograms of rice. Always twenty kilograms.

H2.text: Now you push a box with ten newtons, and a friend pushes with ten newtons too.

H3.text: The total push can be twenty newtons, or zero, or anything between. How?

H4.text: Aarav met the same puzzle on his bicycle.

H5.text: He rode three kilometres east, then four kilometres north. His trip meter says seven.

H6.text: But he is only five kilometres from the college gate. Three plus four makes five? Let's find out.

P1.text: Some quantities need only a size. We call them scalars.

P2.text: Mass, time, temperature, distance. A number and a unit tell the full story.

P3.text: Other quantities need a size and a direction. We call them vectors.

P4.text: Displacement, velocity, acceleration and force are all vectors.

P5.text: And a vector adds by the triangle law, not like plain numbers.

S1.text: Let's replay Aarav's ride on our motion notebook.

S2.text: He sets off east from the gate. The distance counter climbs. One, two, three kilometres.

S3.text: The violet arrow is his displacement. It points from the gate straight to where he is now.

S4.text: Now he turns north. The distance keeps climbing, to seven.

S5.text: Let's replay that turn in slow motion, and watch only the violet arrow.

S6.text: It swings towards north, and it grows. But it stops at five, not seven.

S7.text: On the graph, distance climbs in a straight line. Displacement matches it, then bends below.

M1.text: Freeze at the end. Leg one, three kilometres east. Leg two, four kilometres north.

M2.text: The displacement arrow joins the tail of the first leg to the head of the last.

D1.text: Now the maths, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Distance is a scalar, so it adds like plain numbers. Three plus four is seven kilometres.

D3.text: Step two. The legs meet at a right angle. The displacement is the longest side of a right triangle.

D4.text: Step three. By Pythagoras, s squared equals three squared plus four squared. Nine plus sixteen is twenty five.

D5.text: Step four. So s is five kilometres, pointing about fifty three degrees north of east.

T1.text: Remember this. Scalars add like plain numbers. Vectors add by the triangle law.

K1.text: Side by side. Ten kilograms plus ten kilograms is always twenty kilograms.

K2.text: Ten newtons plus ten newtons, pushing the same way, gives twenty newtons.

K3.text: At a right angle, about fourteen newtons. Pushing against each other, zero.

K4.text: Same numbers, different answers. The direction decides.

K5.text: Now you try. Two pushes of ten newtons act on one box. Can the total push be zero? Pause and decide.

K6.text: Yes! When the two pushes point in opposite directions, they cancel. Mass can never do that.

L1.text: So is a new quantity a scalar or a vector? Follow the links.

L2.text: Speed equals distance divided by time.

L3.text: Distance is a scalar. Time is a scalar. A scalar divided by a scalar is a scalar. So speed is a scalar.

L4.text: Velocity equals displacement divided by time.

L5.text: Displacement is a vector. Dividing by time, a positive number, keeps its direction. So velocity is a vector.

U1.text: One more rule. Two vectors are equal only with the same size and the same direction.

U2.text: Move an arrow without turning it, and it is still the same vector.

U3.text: But five kilometres east and five kilometres north are not equal.

Z1.text: Your turn. Can the size of the displacement ever be bigger than the distance travelled? Pause and decide.

Z2.text: No! A straight line is the shortest path. So displacement can equal distance, but never beat it.

W2.text: A student walks eight metres east, then six metres north. Find the distance and the displacement.

W3.text: Distance is a scalar. Eight plus six is fourteen metres.

W4.text: Displacement is a vector. The legs meet at a right angle, so s squared equals eight squared plus six squared.

W5.text: That is sixty four plus thirty six, which is one hundred. So s is ten metres.

W6.text: Distance, fourteen metres. Displacement, ten metres, pointing north of east.

X2.text: Aarav rides two kilometres to college, and back home. Many students say his distance is zero.

X3.text: Wrong. The distance is four kilometres. It is the displacement that is zero, because he ends where he started.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As quick questions: pick the vector, or find distance and displacement for a path.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A particle moves six metres east, eight metres north, then six metres west. Find the ratio of distance to the size of displacement. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Five to two.

A2.text: Distance is six plus eight plus six, which is twenty metres.

A3.text: East and west cancel. So the displacement is eight metres north.

A4.text: Twenty divided by eight is five over two. Five to two.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. How can ten newtons plus ten newtons give zero?

Y3.text: Two. Is speed a scalar or a vector, and why?

Y4.text: Three. Can displacement ever be bigger than distance?

N1.text: Next time: how do you draw a vector so that anyone can read its size and its direction? We find out in vector representation.
